svg.text: Swizzle<3,3,3> step by step, following one value
The tile: 8 rows × 64 columns of bf16 values (2 bytes each) in shared memory. The value we follow: row 3, column 8.
Slot: where a value sits in shared memory
Shared memory is one long line of numbered places, and the tile is stored in it row after row:
row 0 fills places 0–63, row 1 fills 64–127, and so on. A value's place in that line is its slot:
slot = row × 64 + column. Row 3, column 8 is slot 3 × 64 + 8 = 200.
Each row is cut into 8 chunks of 8 values. 8 bf16 values are 16 bytes, the amount one thread loads
at a time, and the swizzle moves whole chunks. Column 8 is chunk 1, position 0 (its first value).
Light blue: chunk 1 of row 3, its 8 values. Dark blue: its first value, row 3, column 8 = slot 200.
Write the slot in binary: it splits into row, chunk and position
In binary each digit (bit) is worth twice the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... Because a row is 64 = 2⁶ values
and a chunk 8 = 2³, the 9 bits of a slot fall into three groups of 3 that can be read off directly:

svg.text: Row mod 8: the row group has only 3 bits, enough for rows 0–7. The pattern covers 8 rows and then repeats,
so in a taller tile these bits hold the remainder of row ÷ 8, the row mod 8: row 11 reads as 3, row 8 as 0.
The swizzle: XOR the row into the chunk
XOR compares two bits: the same gives 0, different gives 1. Put the row bits over the chunk bits and
XOR each column. Row and position are left as they are; only the chunk number changes.

svg.text: 1 XOR 3 = 2: chunk 1 of row 3 is stored at place 2, where
Row 0 XORs with 000 and never moves. In every other row
the chunks swap places in pairs (row 3: 0 ↔ 3, 1 ↔ 2, ...);
each row still holds all 8 of its own chunks, in a new order.
Do the same for every chunk of row 3
Step 3 moved one chunk. The swizzle does the same XOR for all 8 chunks of the row, always with the same
row number, 011. Each column below is one chunk of row 3:

svg.text: This is row 3 of the right-hand grid in step 5. The chunks swap in pairs: c0 ↔ c3, c1 ↔ c2, c4 ↔ c7, c5 ↔ c6. No two land
on the same place, because XOR can be undone: XOR the place with 011 again and you get the chunk back.
Doing the same with row 0 (000), row 1 (001), ... row 7 (111) fills the other 7 rows of that grid.
Why: the same chunk of 8 rows now sits in 8 different groups of banks
The kernel's loads read the same chunk from 8 rows at the same time, for example chunk 1 of rows 0–7 (blue).
Each place across a row is served by its own group of 4 banks, and one group serves one read at a time.
Each grid below is the 8 rows as stored in memory; each cell says which chunk is stored at that place.

svg.text: Chunk 1 of row r is at place 1 XOR r.
8 reads, 8 different groups of banks: 1 pass.
Orange: row 3, the value from step 3, now at place 2.
Follow chunk 0 instead and the blue cells form a diagonal (place r in row r, as in the smem_layout figure).
Every chunk makes a different pattern, but always 8 different places, so every chunk reads in 1 pass.
How the computer does it: from one slot number to the new slot number
Steps 3–5 describe the rule with a row and a chunk. But when the kernel asks for row 3, column 8, CuTe works
with its slot only: one number goes in (200) and one number must come out (208). There are two ways to do that.
The long way: take the slot apart, do step 3, put it back together

svg.text: (// is division rounded down, % the remainder.) This works, but it needs divisions and multiplications,
and it pulls the slot apart into three separate numbers only to glue them back together.
The short way: change only the chunk bits, right inside the slot
Step 2 showed that the slot's bits already are row | chunk | position, side by side. Only the 3 chunk bits must
change, and XOR with 0 changes nothing. So build a number that holds the row in the chunk's place and 0s
everywhere else (000 011 000), then XOR the whole slot with it. The row and position bits meet 0s and stay as
they are; the chunk bits meet the row bits, which is exactly step 3. In code, with S = 3 and M = 3:

svg.text: >> 3 slides every bit 3 places to the right; << 3 slides 3 places to the left; & keeps a bit only where both numbers
have a 1; ^ is XOR; 0b111 is binary 111. Read it from the inside out (colours show where each bit came from):

svg.text: chunk 1 → 2 (step 3); the rest met 0s and stayed
Same answer both ways: 208. The short way is the long way squeezed into 3 bit operations: no division,
no multiplication, and the slot never has to be taken apart. This one line is what Swizzle<3,3,3> is.
So what the three numbers of Swizzle<B, M, S> count

svg.text: how many bits get changed: the chunk number. 2³ = 8 chunks per row, and the pattern spans 8 rows.

text.font-family: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'DejaVu Sans Mono', monospace

svg.text: how many low bits are never touched: the position. 2³ = 8 values, so a 16-byte chunk moves whole.

text.font-family: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'DejaVu Sans Mono', monospace

svg.text: how far above the chunk bits the row bits start: bit M + S = 6, since a row is 2⁶ = 64 values.
